li.a: The Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan: Frog Lake Massacre
Dictionary of Canadian Biography: Kapapamahchakwew (Wandering Spirit), by Sylvia M. Van Kirk
The Globe and Mail: I thought I knew the bloody saga of Frog Lake. Then I learned another side of the story
CBC News: 140 years after Frog Lake Massacre, Cree community hopes to reshape tale of 1885 resistance
Saskatchewan Indian, July 1972: Battleford Hangings, 1885 Riel Rebellion
Elk Point Historical Society: Frog Lake Massacre 1885

content.p: On the morning of 2 April 1885, a party of Plains Cree warriors seized the small government and mission settlement of Frog Lake, in what was then the North-West Territories, and nine men were dead by the end of the morning. They included the Indian agent, Thomas Quinn, and two Roman Catholic priests. The killings were led by a war chief named Wandering Spirit, against the wishes of the chief whose band he belonged to, Big Bear.

The Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan calls the episode one of the most influential events of the North-West Resistance, though it was not a military engagement, and says it was incited by hunger and mistreatment rather than politics. Eight Cree men were hanged at Fort Battleford that November, six of them for Frog Lake. The name "massacre" has stuck, but Cree speakers quoted by CBC in 2025 say the story has been told from one side only.

The Plains Cree who gathered around Big Bear had watched their world collapse in the 1870s. The Dictionary of Canadian Biography describes the disappearance of the buffalo and the signing of the treaties as a source of particular bitterness and despair for war leaders such as Wandering Spirit. Big Bear's followers held out against the new order until starvation forced them to take Treaty 6 in December 1882. The Globe and Mail adds that Big Bear had been the last of the plains chiefs to make a treaty, and that even then he resisted settling on a reserve, leading his people between the North-West and Montana until they fetched up at Frog Lake. Along the way, the newspaper says, he lost much of his authority to younger and more militant men who blamed him for their condition.

Wandering Spirit was one of them. Born around 1845, he had risen to be war chief, an office separate from Big Bear's social leadership, through daring in battle. The biography says he was reputed to have killed between 11 and 13 Blackfoot warriors, more than any other man in the band, and says the war chief also headed the warrior society, whose duties included policing the camps and special tasks in the buffalo hunt.

In the winter of 1884 to 1885, the destitute band camped near Frog Lake, which was a Department of Indian Affairs agency as well as a Catholic mission. The Globe and Mail says the settlement had by then added a church, a school, a store, a sawmill and a police barracks. The winter was harsh, the paper says, and the people in the Cree camps were starving. Quinn, in charge of the agency, was stingy with the rations he was supposed to hand out in return for work such as cutting firewood. The Dictionary of Canadian Biography says militants such as Wandering Spirit grew increasingly hostile to his strict enforcement of a "no work, no ration" policy.

Another current ran through the camp. According to the same biography, the band had met Louis Riel in Montana in the early 1880s, and he had urged that Métis and Indians together could drive the Canadians out and regain their freedom. When news arrived in late March that the Métis had routed the North-West Mounted Police at Duck Lake, Big Bear was, in the biography's words, powerless to stop Wandering Spirit and the other warriors from attacking Frog Lake.

The Elk Point Historical Society says that on 2 April Wandering Spirit and his young warriors collected the guns of the white men at the settlement, and that the six Mounted Police stationed there had left shortly before, as a goodwill gesture, because it was thought the Cree would not attack if the police were gone. The Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan says a party of warriors captured Quinn at his home before dawn. According to the Dictionary of Canadian Biography, the 12 whites and mixed-bloods in Frog Lake were rounded up while the Cree ransacked the Hudson's Bay Company store and the police barracks. The Globe and Mail says the attackers arrived with their faces painted for war.

The accounts then differ in their detail. The Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan says the prisoners were ordered to move to an encampment about 2 kilometres away shortly before 11 a.m., and that Quinn stubbornly refused, whereupon Wandering Spirit shot him in the head. The Dictionary of Canadian Biography likewise says Quinn's defiant refusal to go to the Indian camp so enraged Wandering Spirit that he shot him, then shouted for the death of all whites. The Elk Point account has most of the white people herded into the church for a short service before Wandering Spirit decided to move them, and says Quinn was shot near his own home after a disagreement. The Globe and Mail tells it differently: it says the attackers shot John Delaney dead at his wife's side, then shot the priest Adelarde Fafard as he leaned over to give last rites, and does not mention Quinn's refusal.

The sources agree on nine dead and on who they were. Besides Quinn, the dead were John Gowanlock, who ran the sawmill; John Delaney, a farming instructor; the priests Leon Fafard and Felix Marchand; the clerk William Gilchrist; the trader George Dill; the carpenter Charles Gouin; and John Williscroft, Father Fafard's lay assistant.

Some people were spared. The Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan says Cree women hid William Cameron, a Hudson's Bay clerk, under a large shawl, and the Elk Point society adds that Edward Dufresne, an interpreter married to a Cree woman, also survived. Theresa Delaney and Theresa Gowanlock, who had each just lost a husband, were taken prisoner. The Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan puts the number of captives, including families and others from the settlement, at 70. The buildings of the settlement were burned to their foundations, the Globe and Mail says.

The role of Big Bear's son Ayimâsis, spelled Imasees in some places, is described differently. The Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan says he and Wandering Spirit led the Cree party. The Elk Point account calls him a shadowy figure who urged the killings but did not take part in them and escaped retribution.
content.h2: Captivity, and the war that followed
content.p: The two widows spent weeks travelling the prairie with Big Bear, Wandering Spirit and the band as Canadian forces sent west to crush the rebellion moved against the camp. The Globe and Mail says the press ran lurid stories that they were suffering "a fate worse than death", but that in fact they came to no physical harm. They were looked after by John Pritchard, a Métis man who had interpreted at Frog Lake, and in the end they got away from the moving camp and reached safety. Their joint book, Two Months in the Camp of Big Bear, appeared within a few months.

Wandering Spirit stayed prominent. According to the Dictionary of Canadian Biography, in his speeches before the fall of Fort Pitt in mid April he declared that the Cree were "tired of him [the government] and all his people". Big Bear's intervention at Fort Pitt is credited with preventing another violent outburst that might have cost the white captives their lives. On 28 May the war chief rallied the camp at Frenchman Butte when General Strange's forces interrupted a Thirst Dance, and the Cree repelled the attack. Afterwards the Wood Cree deserted Big Bear, and a dramatic change seems to have come over Wandering Spirit. Burdened with remorse, in the biography's account, he tried to kill himself with a chest wound as the Wood Cree surrendered at Fort Pitt. He told Cameron later: "I knew there was no hope for me. Perhaps, I thought, if I sacrificed myself the government would not be so hard on the rest." He survived and was carried by stretcher to Battleford to be tried.

The Dictionary of Canadian Biography calls the trials short and, in retrospect, arbitrary. The accused had no legal counsel, and the magistrate who heard every case was Charles-Borromée Rouleau, a stipendiary magistrate. Wandering Spirit admitted that he shot Quinn but would not explain why, and on 22 September he was sentenced to hang.

The next person the biography says was found guilty of murder was Round the Sky, accused of shooting Father Fafard after the priest had been wounded by Wandering Spirit. The biography says one account claimed he had been cared for by the priest and was goaded into it by his comrades' taunts, but no such evidence was heard in court. On 3 October Miserable Man and Bad Arrow were tried for the killing of Charles Gouin and pleaded not guilty. Miserable Man asked Cameron to confirm his alibi that he had been in the Hudson's Bay store at the time; Cameron, who the biography says loathed him, had already helped the Crown obtain evidence from Indian witnesses who claimed that Wandering Spirit ordered Bad Arrow to shoot Gouin, and that Miserable Man shot him as well.

The biographer judges the case against Little Bear and Iron Body, for the killing of George Dill, unconvincing in retrospect. Iron Body was convicted on Little Bear's evidence, and Little Bear was then convicted too, yet both firmly denied firing the fatal shot, and Iron Body said an Indian who had escaped custody had shot Dill. "It seems that the federal government was determined to make an example of these Indians," the biography concludes. When the justice minister, John Sparrow David Thompson, reviewed the cases, he considered no mitigating circumstances and the sentences stood.

The Saskatchewan Indian magazine, in a 1972 account, lists the six convicted for Frog Lake with their alleged offences. Wandering Spirit was convicted for the killing of Quinn, Walking the Sky for Father Fafard (the Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan lists him under the same name; none of the saved pages says whether he is the Round the Sky of the biography), Bad Arrow and Miserable Man for Gouin, and Iron Body and Little Bear for Dill. The same account names two more men sentenced to hang that autumn: Crooked Leg, for the killing of a farm instructor named Payne, and Man Without Blood, for the killing of a rancher named Tremont. The Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan says two Cree men were condemned for a murder committed on 29 March, just before the Siege of Battleford.

The eight were executed together at 8 o'clock that morning on a scaffold built in the barrack square at Fort Battleford, the 1972 magazine account says, with a police squad forming a cordon at its foot. It says the condemned were given ten minutes to speak and that all but Wandering Spirit did so. Little Bear, in the speech the magazine prints, said: "I never thought to lift my hand against a white man." The Dictionary of Canadian Biography adds that, according to legend, Wandering Spirit chanted a love song to his wife softly while others shouted war cries. Cameron had interviewed him the previous day, when he said he regretted believing the Indians could resist the whites and restore the old way of life, and begged not to be buried in the ball and chain that shackled him.

The magazine reports that the Indian pupils of the Battleford Industrial School were taken out to witness it, the magazine says, as a lasting reminder of what happened to those who made trouble with the Crown. The bodies went into a common grave on the hillside, later covered by an unmarked concrete slab. The Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan describes the hangings as the largest mass execution in Canadian history.
content.h2: Big Bear and the people left behind
content.p: Big Bear had not been at the killings; the Elk Point account says he did not want war. The Globe and Mail says he was hunted down, put in irons and sentenced to jail for treason, was released after 18 months, and died a year later, "a broken and sick man", as the Canadian Encyclopedia put it. The Globe and Mail says that most of the people left at Frog Lake ended up on reserves, the fate Big Bear had resisted.

The political fallout was lasting. The Globe and Mail argues that Frog Lake ended any notion that the future of the West might be shared between newcomers and the original inhabitants, and quotes Prime Minister John A. Macdonald telling Parliament, "we must teach the Indians what law is." It quotes the historian Sarah Carter, who wrote in 1997 that Theresa Delaney's captivity story helped justify the hangings and "to sanction the series of repressive measures" that followed in the West. The paper's own columnist, a relative of Delaney's, calls the book colonial propaganda.

The same article reports that John Delaney had a reputation for exploiting Cree women. It cites Big Bear's biographer Hugh Dempsey, who wrote that he was among those who "prostituted their authority to the debauchery of young Indian women". According to a scholarly paper by Christine Yvonne Martineau, a Cree woman named Genevieve Missinabiskop was pregnant when she fled Frog Lake after the killings, and gave birth to a daughter, Marguerite, known as Maggie, whom a baptismal certificate of 20 May 1886 records as the illegitimate child of Genevieve and John Delaney. Maggie grew up to marry a Métis man and had a large family. Her descendants include a Calgary artist, Sarah Houle, who is making an art project about 1885.

Frog Lake is also remembered by Cree communities in a different way from the old accounts. Before the 140th anniversary events planned for St. Paul, Alberta, in 2025, Leah Redcrow of Saddle Lake Cree Nation, chief executive of the Acimowin Opaspiw Society, told CBC that her Snake Hills band was blamed for the entire rebellion because of Frog Lake, and that much of the historical record is "grossly incorrect". She said it has long been known in her community that Wandering Spirit was not killed but escaped to the United States, and that about 500 people from her band fled and set up what became the Rocky Boy reservation in Montana. Jonathan Windy Boy, a Montana state senator and a descendant, said: "If he got hung, I wouldn't be here." The grave marker at Fort Battleford National Historic Site carries Wandering Spirit's name; CBC reports that at some point it was installed and that Parks Canada did not respond to its request for comment. The Dictionary of Canadian Biography and the other written sources used here record his hanging as fact.

The Cree elder Eric Tootoosis, of Poundmaker Cree Nation, told CBC that the anniversary is a time to give thanks for survival. He said much has changed, pointing to the exoneration and apology given to Chief Poundmaker, who was convicted of treason-felony. At the Frog Lake site itself, the Globe and Mail writer found a fieldstone cairn and two short lines of rusting crosses, each bearing a name and the word "massacred", and noted that Quinn's picture had been vandalized on one of the Frog Lake signs.
